name: Thaddaeus (Judas of James)
title: One of the Twelve
tagline: Two names in the lists, and one question at the Last Supper.
story: Named Thaddaeus in the lists of Matthew and Mark; Luke and Acts have no Thaddaeus but list "Judas the brother of James"; Scripture says little more.

entries.title: “Judas of James”
entries.text: Luke and Acts name him by his relation to a James. The Greek gives only the genitive, literally Judas of James; the KJV prints “the brother” as a supplied word, and the Revised Version of 1881 reads the son of James. Who this James was, Scripture does not say.

entries.title: In the upper room
entries.text: He is named with the other apostles in the upper room after the ascension.

entries.title: Never named again
entries.text: The last verse that names him is Acts 1:13. After that Acts speaks of “the eleven” and “the twelve” as a body (Acts 2:14; 6:2) but never names him again.

entries.title: Eusebius, Church History 1.13.4
entries.text: Eusebius says that after the ascension Thomas sent “Thaddeus, who was also numbered among the seventy disciples of Christ” to King Abgar at Edessa, translating the story from Syriac records he says were kept there. Eusebius counts this Thaddaeus among the Seventy, not the Twelve; McGiffert (1890) calls that an error and notes that Eusebius is the first known to tell the story.

entries.title: Acts of the Holy Apostle Thaddaeus (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 8)
entries.text: The Greek “Acts of the Holy Apostle Thaddaeus” makes him one of the Twelve, born at Edessa; after preaching in Syria he “fell asleep” at Berytus (Beirut) and was buried there.
entries.who: Acts of the Holy Apostle Thaddaeus (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 8)
entries.when: date not established; one manuscript's title calls him “one of the seventy”

verses.text: Now the names of the twelve apostles are these; The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;
Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.
And Simon he surnamed Peter;
And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder:
And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Canaanite,
And Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him: and they went into an house.
Simon, (whom he also named Peter,) and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew,
Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphæus, and Simon called Zelotes,
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.

And when they were come in, they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James.

verses.text: And he goeth up into a mountain, and calleth unto him whom he would: and they came unto him.
And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach,
And to have power to heal sicknesses, and to cast out devils:
And Simon he surnamed Peter;
And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder:
And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Canaanite,
And Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him: and they went into an house.
And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God.
¶ And when it was day, he called unto him his disciples: and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles;
Simon, (whom he also named Peter,) and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew,
Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphæus, and Simon called Zelotes,
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.

items.q: Are Thaddaeus and Judas of James one man?
items.full: Are Thaddaeus and Judas of James one man? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: One man
views.holders: Jerome, Commentary on Matthew (late 4th century), as reported by McGiffert and Kerr; A. C. McGiffert (1890); C. M. Kerr, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Each stands in the third group of four (tenth in Matthew and Mark, eleventh in Luke and Acts), and no list has both names.

views.label: Two men
views.holders: Ewald and others, as reported by C. M. Kerr (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: On this view Thaddaeus died during Jesus' lifetime and Judas was chosen in his place.

views.label: A Thaddaeus of the Seventy
views.holders: Eusebius, Church History 1.12.3 and 1.13 (about AD 325), reporting what “they say”

argument.text: Eusebius counts the Thaddaeus sent to Edessa among the seventy disciples, not the Twelve. McGiffert (1890) calls this an error like the one that made Cephas a different man from Peter.

items.q: Was he the brother of James, or the son of James?
items.full: Was he the brother of James, or the son of James? (In the order the readings appeared in English.)

views.label: Brother of James
views.holders: the KJV translators (1611), who supplied “the brother”; Jacobus de Voragine (about 1260), who calls him “brother to James the Less”

argument.text: The letter of Jude opens with a Jude who is “brother of James”; read beside that verse, the supplied word “brother” fits.

views.label: Son of James
views.holders: the Revised Version (1881); C. M. Kerr, ISBE (1915): “The latter is to be preferred”

argument.text: The Greek has the same bare genitive as for James of Alphaeus in the verse before, where the KJV itself supplies “the son”.

items.q: Is he Jude, the Lord's brother and the writer of the letter of Jude?
items.full: Is he Jude, the Lord's brother and the writer of the letter of Jude? (In the order the sources give them.)

argument.text: The writer of Jude calls himself “brother of James”, and the Lord's brothers included a James and a Judas.

views.label: No
views.holders: A. C. McGiffert (1890); C. M. Kerr, ISBE (1915); Easton himself under “Lebbaeus”

argument.text: John says the Lord's brothers did not believe in him, and if Luke means son of James, this Judas cannot be the Jude who is “brother of James”.

items.q: Why two names in the lists?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: This page treats Thaddaeus (Matthew 10, Mark 3) and Judas of James (Luke 6, Acts 1) as one man: each stands in the third group of four (tenth in Matthew and Mark, eleventh in Luke and Acts), and no list has both names. Jerome (as McGiffert and Kerr report), McGiffert (1890) and Kerr (ISBE, 1915) hold this; Kerr calls it “generally accepted”.

items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: John's “Judas … not Iscariot” at the Last Supper is taken to be this Judas, the only other Judas in the lists.

items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: The texts differ at Matthew 10:3. The KJV, following the Textus Receptus, reads “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus”; Tischendorf's Greek text (1869-72) has “Lebbaeus” alone, and the Revised Version (1881) “Thaddaeus” alone.

items.from: Asked on the James, Peter & Jude page

views.label: The brother of Jesus and of James
views.holders: J. B. Mayor (1907), Charles Bigg (1901), the ISBE

argument.text: The same family list names "James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon". Mayor thought Jude probably the youngest or next to youngest of the Lord's brothers. Eusebius, from Hegesippus, tells how the grandsons of Jude — who was said to have been the Lord's brother in the flesh — were brought before the emperor Domitian and released when they showed hands hardened by farm work.

views.label: The apostle "Judas of James", one of the Twelve
views.holders: Easton's Bible Dictionary (1897); Calvin treats Jude as an apostle

argument.text: Luke lists "Judas the brother of James" among the Twelve — apparently the man also called Thaddaeus or Lebbaeus. In the KJV the words "the brother" are supplied; the Greek has only "Judas of James", which can also mean "son of James".

views.label: A later Judas
views.holders: Grotius (Judas, a later bishop of Jerusalem); Harnack ("brother of James" added between 150 and 180); Jülicher (a writer from a circle that honoured James) — all as reported by Bigg

argument.text: These proposals follow from dating the letter in the second century; Bigg remarked that they rest on that assumption.
